title: the Arthashastra's opening
tomorrow: balance all three aims, then crown one of them. which one?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Arthashastra's opening kept its king a student: vinaya, rooted in the elders. Today, the king at work, and someone at his door.

The man at the palace gate has been there since morning. He's holding a rolled-up complaint about a field boundary, and the guard has already told him twice: the king is busy, come back later. Behind him a widow is waiting with a grandson, and behind her someone sick enough to need a hand to stand. The sun moves. Nobody comes out. Inside, the Arthashastra has an opinion about this scene, and it isn't on the guard's side.
screen: `WAITING SINCE MORNING.` → `COME BACK LATER.` → `NOBODY COMES OUT.`

segments.voice: In its chapter on the king's duties, the book says a ruler must not keep a petitioner waiting at the door. When he makes himself hard to reach, it warns, business gets tangled and the people turn against him. So he hears cases himself, and promptly. It even names whose matters come first, among them children, the old, the sick and the helpless: the people in that line. An urgent case heard late, it says, can become hard or impossible to set right. Then comes a verse worth slowing down for. In the happiness of his subjects lies the king's happiness. In their welfare, his welfare. What pleases the king himself, he should not count as good. What pleases his people, that is good. That's the story's ending, written as a rule. The gate opens, and the ones who can least afford to wait go first. It's a long way from a king's comfort. The book that began with a pond, where the rod protects the small fish, now moves the king's happiness out of the palace and into the line at his gate.
screen: `DON'T KEEP PEOPLE AT THE DOOR.` · `THE YOUNG, OLD, SICK AND HELPLESS FIRST.` · `LATE CAN MEAN TOO LATE.` · `THEIR HAPPINESS IS HIS.` · then, large: `WHAT PLEASES HIS PEOPLE IS GOOD.`

segments.voice: On paper or in a note, write the name of one person who's been waiting on you: for a reply, a visit, a little attention. Under it, write one word for what they're waiting for. Then breathe slowly with the page in front of you, and let their good matter to you as much as your own.
The Arthashastra's opening: a king who doesn't keep people at the gate, and finds his happiness in theirs.
Your line: the Arthashastra's opening. In the people's happiness is the king's. See you tomorrow.

fork.reveal: the Arthashastra names the old, the sick and the helpless among those whose matters can't be put off, and warns that late can become too late.
